summary: For ages 7-8, model real-world measurement, money, and time problems by choosing and justifying a representation (bar model, number line, or equation), carrying multi-step calculations with units attached, and crucially interpreting the final number as the RIGHT quantity (total cost vs change). The signature hazard is suspension of sense-making: computing to a number without naming which quantity the question asked for or checking its reasonableness. Line plots extend modelling to reading answers off a data display.
misconceptions: Reports the wrong quantity — gives the total cost when the question asks for the change
Stops after the first step of a multi-step problem
Computes without sense-checking whether the answer is reasonable in context
Drops or muddles units (mixing pounds and pence, or minutes and hours)

activities.title: Multi-step money modeller: name the quantity, then check it
steps: Set up a shopping problem: two items at 65p and 20p, paying with £1
Choose a representation and say why it fits (e.g. a bar model with a £1 whole, an 85p part for the shopping, and a mystery part)
Pause at the interim number and label it: 'that 85p — what is it?' Answer: the total cost (65p + 20p = 85p)
Carry on to the second step: change £1 into 100p, then work out 100p − 85p = 15p as the change
Interpret the final number with its unit ('15p change') and sense-check it: the cost and the change together should make the £1 paid (85p + 15p = 100p = £1)
Transfer: re-run the model paying with £2 instead and describe what changes
activities.insight: In a multi-step problem each number along the way means something specific; the answer is only right when you name the quantity the question actually asked for and check it is reasonable in context.

activities.title: Shopkeeper who tries it on (spoken correction)
steps: Play out a shop exchange where a shopkeeper rings up two items and states the subtotal as if it were the change
Catch and correct the error out loud, explaining which quantity the stated number actually is
Keep units straight (pounds and pence) while justifying the fix
Explain aloud how a bar or equation would separate the cost from the change
activities.insight: Distinguishing which quantity the answer names is a reasoning skill you can articulate and defend, not just compute.

activities.title: Worked multi-step walkthrough (scaffold)
steps: Step through a worked multi-step money or measurement problem
Reveal what each step's number means (e.g. tap a step to show 'this is the total cost', 'this is the change')
Describe in your own words what the interim number means before seeing the next step
activities.insight: Each number in a worked solution carries a meaning; following the labels shows how an interim quantity differs from the final answer.

activities.title: Line plot from measurement data
steps: Collect or receive measurement data (e.g. lengths of objects)
Create a line plot displaying the data
Use the plot to answer a real-world question, reading the answer off the display back into the situation
State what quantity your answer represents and whether it is reasonable
activities.insight: A data display is a representation you read answers from; the answer must be interpreted back into the real-world question with its units.

checkQuestion: In a shop you buy two things: one costs 65p and one costs 20p. You pay with a £1 coin. A friend works it out and says 'the answer is 85'. Is 85 the change? Talk me through the problem — what does 85 mean, what is the change, and how do you know your change makes sense?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising 85p is the TOTAL COST (an interim quantity), computing the change as 100 − 85 = 15p, interpreting it as '15p change', and sense-checking that the change is less than the £1 paid.
